Escape
es-kape'
v. and n. (to get free of a danger; a way out; rendering Hebrew malat and palat, Greek ekpheugo and ekbasis)
From Old French eschaper, from a late Latin excappare, to slip out of one's cape — to leave the cloak in the pursuer's hand and get away. The image of a garment abandoned to escape is exactly Joseph's in Genesis 39.

Biblical Definition

Escape in Scripture is urgent, provided, and in one case impossible. It is urgent at Sodom, where the angels give Lot a command with no room in it: “Escape for thy life; look not behind thee, neither stay thou in all the plain; escape to the mountain, lest thou be consumed” (Genesis 19:17). Four imperatives, and one of them was disobeyed by his wife. It is provided in temptation: “God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it” (1 Corinthians 10:13) — and the promise is precise. The way out is made with the temptation, so it exists at the time it is needed, and its purpose is stated as endurance rather than avoidance. The Psalter sings of escape already granted: “Our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers: the snare is broken, and we are escaped” (Psalm 124:7) — and the deliverance is credited to the snare being broken, not to the bird's strength. Against all of these Hebrews sets the one danger with no exit: “How shall we escape, if we neglect so great salvation” (Hebrews 2:3). The verse is a question because there is no answer to it. Neglect is enough; no active rejection is required.

Webster 1828 Definition

To get free of danger. Lot is commanded to escape with four imperatives; God makes a way to escape with every temptation; the soul escapes as a bird when the snare is broken — and Hebrews asks how we shall escape if we neglect so great salvation.

expand to see more

ESCAPE, v.t. [Fr. echapper; It. scappare.] To flee from and avoid; to get out of the way; to shun.

2. To pass without harm; as, the ship escaped the storm.

3. ESCAPE, v.i. To flee, shun and be secure from danger; to avoid an evil.

4. ESCAPE, n. Flight to shun danger or injury; the act of fleeing from danger.

5. Excuse; subterfuge; evasion. In Scripture, a way to escape, 1 Cor. 10.

Key Scripture

Genesis 19:17 — "And it came to pass, when they had brought them forth abroad, that he said, Escape for thy life; look not behind thee, neither stay thou in all the plain; escape to the mountain, lest thou be consumed."

1 Corinthians 10:13 — "There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it."

Psalm 124:7 — "Our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers: the snare is broken, and we are escaped."

Hebrews 2:3 — "How shall we escape, if we neglect so great salvation; which at the first began to be spoken by the Lord, and was confirmed unto us by them that heard him;"

Modern Corruption

1 Corinthians 10:13 is quoted as a promise that God will not give more than a man can handle — a saying about circumstances the verse never makes, since it speaks of temptation and promises endurance rather than relief.

expand to see more

The popular version of this verse — God will not give you more than you can handle — is not what Paul wrote and does not survive contact with 2 Corinthians 1:8, where the same apostle says he was pressed out of measure, above strength, insomuch that he despaired even of life. The promise of 1 Corinthians 10:13 is about temptation, that is, solicitation to sin, and it makes three specific claims: the temptation is common to man, God limits it, and he supplies a way of escape. It does not promise that afflictions will stay within a believer's capacity. In fact Paul says the crushing weight he bore was given that we should not trust in ourselves, but in God which raiseth the dead. Comfort misquoted collapses at the moment it is most needed.

The principle to recover is the weight of Hebrews 2:3. The word is neglect, and it names the way most people are lost — not by argument or defiance but by never getting round to it. The letter is written to people who had heard, who had been confirmed in it by eyewitnesses, and who were drifting; the previous verse spoke of letting things slip. There is no answer to the question how shall we escape, because the salvation neglected is the only escape there is. A man who declines a lifeboat has not thereby found a better one.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew malat is to slip away, to be delivered; palat, to bring to safety. Greek ekpheugo is to flee out of; ekbasis, a way out, the word in 1 Corinthians 10:13.

expand to see more

Hebrew malat (H4422) — to slip away, escape, be delivered; the angels' command to Lot.

Hebrew palat (H6403) — to escape, to bring to safety; the root of peleitah, a remnant escaped.

Greek ekpheugo (G1628) — to flee out, to escape; how shall we escape, Hebrews 2:3.

Greek ekbasis (G1545) — a way out, an issue; the way to escape of 1 Corinthians 10:13.

Greek peirasmos (G3986) — a trial, a temptation; what the way of escape is provided with.

Usage

"Of urgent flight: escape for thy life; look not behind thee (Genesis 19:17)."

"Of the escape provided with temptation: will with the temptation also make a way to escape (1 Corinthians 10:13)."

"Of the danger with no exit: how shall we escape, if we neglect so great salvation (Hebrews 2:3)."
